solution:
Shamrao should send his crop to the nearest sugar mill on the map.

The factor that decides it is the nature of the raw material. The chapter explains that sugarcane loses weight and amount of sugar after harvesting as the time after harvest increases, which affects its effective use for producing sugar, so sugarcane needs to be sent to nearby factories as soon as possible.

That is why sugar industries are located near the production of the raw material in the first place. Sugarcane is a weight-losing raw material, and the chapter states that weight-losing industries are located near the raw material.

The factors Shamrao will weigh are therefore distance to the mill, the time the journey takes, the transport cost for a heavy and bulky crop, and the price the mill offers.

The son is correct. The bakery should be in the city.

The chapter uses this very example: in bakery industries the final output, say cake, has higher weight than the raw materials, and this will be costlier to transport because transport cost increases with weight. Therefore bakery industries are located near the markets.

A bakery is a weight-gaining industry, and the chapter's rule is that weight-gaining industries will be located near the market while weight-losing industries will be located near the raw material.

The market matters for a second reason as well. Bakery products are perishable, and the chapter notes that a ready market is most essential for perishable and heavy commodities.

Either will do, and that is the point of the example. Shantaram can set the unit up in the village, where he already owns land and the honeycombs are.

The chapter says so directly: the honey industry is a footloose industry, as its location is not related to the weight of the raw material or of the finished product.

Honey neither loses nor gains weight in processing, so neither the raw-material rule nor the market rule pulls it in a particular direction. The chapter adds that footloose industries produce goods that are lightweight and can easily be transported to the markets, and that most of them produce low-volume, high-value outputs.

So the choice can be made on other grounds: he already has his own land in the village, which saves capital, and the source of the honey is there.

Market-oriented industries are those whose finished product is heavier, bulkier or more perishable than the raw material, so that the cost falls on carrying the product rather than the material.

The chapter's own example is the bakery industry: cake as a final product is heavier than the raw materials, which is why such industries are located near markets, that is near cities.

By the same reasoning the chapter's category of weight-gaining industries is market-oriented as a class, because their raw materials are lighter but their finished products are heavier and bulky.

[Note: the chapter gives only the bakery example of a market-oriented industry, so any further example would be supplied from outside it. The test to apply is the one the chapter gives: compare the weight and perishability of the finished product with those of the raw material.]

| Name of Industry | Raw materials required | Finished products | Factor affecting location | Footloose? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cotton textile industries | Raw cotton | Cloth | Humid climate, and cheap transport for a light non-perishable raw material | No |
| Cement industries | Limestone | Cement | Located near the raw material, which is heavy and bulky | No |
| Diamond cutting industries | Rough diamonds | Cut and polished diamonds | Skilled labour; the material is light and of high value | Yes |
| Mobile manufacturing units | Components made elsewhere | Mobile phones | Split location; parts are made in different areas and assembled at one place | Yes |
| Paper industry | Pulpwood | Paper | Located near the forest or reachable by cheap water transport | No |
| Sugar industry | Sugarcane | Sugar | Located near the raw material, which loses weight and sugar after harvest | No |
| Food processing industry | Perishable farm produce | Processed food | Located near the raw material, which is perishable | No |
| IT (Hardware) industry | Light components | Hardware | Skilled labour; low volume and high value output | Yes |
| Oil refinery | Crude oil | Petroleum products | Located near the port or the oilfield; the material is bulky | No |
| Hairpins industry | Small quantities of wire | Hairpins | Neither raw material nor product is bulky | Yes |

The test the chapter gives is whether the location is related to the weight of the raw material or of the finished product. Where it is not, the industry is footloose, and the chapter notes that most footloose industries produce low-volume, high-value outputs that are lightweight and easily transported to markets.

[Note: the chapter names only the honey processing unit as a footloose industry. The verdicts above apply its weight-losing, weight-gaining and footloose definitions to the ten industries listed; the chapter itself classifies none of them.]

The northern hemisphere. Almost every shaded industrial region on the map lies north of the equator, and the great majority of them between 30 degrees N and 60 degrees N. The southern hemisphere carries only a few: parts of Brazil, Argentina and Chile, the mining regions of southern Africa, and the coasts of Australia and the islands south-east of it.

Mainly in the north-eastern part of the continent. The map names New England, New York, the Mid-Atlantic Region and southern Canada there, clustered around the Great Lakes and the Atlantic coast.

A second belt lies on the Pacific side, named on the map as the Western Region (Pacific Coastal Region) and the N.W. Region, with a further region in Eastern Texas.

The chapter's table gives the reasons for the north-east: rich reserves of mineral resources, large rivers and the Great Lakes, a broken coastline, the location of North America and Europe facing each other across the Atlantic, huge capital, a vast market and the development of inland water, rail transport and ports.

Mainly in western Europe and in European Russia.

In western Europe the map names the Great Britain Region, the Ruhr Region and Italy, with the Scandinavian countries to the north. In European Russia it names the Moscow-Tula-Vladimir triangle, the Ural-Volga Region and the North Caucasus Region.

The chapter's table gives western Europe's advantages as the River Rhine, large coal and iron reserves, natural harbours, skilled labour, a large market, port facilities and the development of rail and road transport.

Because the interior of Africa lacks most of the conditions the chapter lists for industrial location.

Transport is the first of them. The chapter states that low cost of transportation is the key factor in the location of industries, and the interior is far from ports, so both raw materials coming in and finished goods going out cost more to move.

Capital is the second. The chapter notes that industries are located where banking and financial facilities are easily available, and that capital is attracted to areas where industries are already localised, which leaves regions with no industry at a standing disadvantage.

Market is the third. Nearness to market is essential for quick disposal of manufactured goods, and the interior has neither the dense population nor the purchasing power that a large market means.

The few interior regions the map does name, Ghana, Congo, Zambia, Kimberley and Witwatersrand, are mineral-based, which fits the chapter's point that industries dependent on heavy and bulky raw materials are located near the raw material area. Elsewhere the coast wins for the reasons given in the next answer.

[Note: the chapter does not discuss Africa's industrial geography in its own right, so the reasons above apply its general location factors to the pattern the map shows.]

The map names five concentrations in India: the Chhota Nagpur Plateau, the Mumbai-Pune corridor, the Ahmedabad-Vadodara region, the Coimbatore-Bangalore region, and the Delhi region.

The chapter's table lists the same set and gives the reasons: rich mineral resources, port facilities available, a hot climate, a large market, a huge supply of labour, an excellent rail network and port facility. Its major industries are textiles, chemicals, food processing, steel, transportation equipment, cement, mining, petroleum, machinery, software and pharmaceuticals.

Because a coast supplies several of the location factors at once.

Transport is the chief one. The chapter states that low cost of transportation is the key factor in the location of industries, and that light-weight and non-perishable items can be brought from far distances through cheaper transportation like waterways, so such industries may be located near ports or rivers, giving cotton textiles and pulpwood as examples.

Ports also give access to markets abroad. The chapter lists export facilities and port facilities among the human factors for North America, Europe and Japan alike, and notes for Japan that the port city of Yokohama facilitates trade.

A broken coastline helps, because it provides natural harbours; the chapter lists it as a physical factor for North America, western Europe and Japan.

Water itself is needed. Almost all industries require plenty of water for cooling, smelting and washing.

Finally, coastal areas are usually the most populous and best connected parts of a country, so they supply both the labour and the market that the chapter names among the human factors.

Industry is concentrated in a single broad latitudinal band, roughly between 30 degrees N and 60 degrees N, and is thin everywhere else.

Within that band lie almost all the great regions the map names: the north-east of North America, western Europe, European Russia, the Manchurian and Vladivostok regions, Korea, Japan, the east coast and Lower Yangtze of China, and northern India. The band is the temperate zone of the northern hemisphere.

South of the equator the map shows only scattered regions, in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, southern Africa, Australia and the islands south-east of it, and most of those lie in the corresponding temperate band between 30 and 40 degrees S.

In the tropics industry is sparse and mostly mineral-based, and in the far north, beyond about 60 degrees N, it is almost absent apart from the Siberian Region.

The chapter's reasoning explains the band. Harsh climate is not much suitable for the establishment of industries, and there may not be any industrial development in extremely hot, humid, dry or cold climate, while a moderate climate is congenial to it. But latitude is not the whole story: the chapter notes that industries tend to concentrate in a few pockets because of favourable factors, and those factors include capital, labour, market and transport as much as climate. The pattern is really one of temperate, densely populated, well connected coasts rather than of latitude as such.

Forest-based industries, above all timber, pulp and paper.

The lumbering map in fig. 4.1 shows the northernmost island of Japan lying in the coniferous forest belt, where the chapter's account of lumbering says only one species of trees is found in an area and the trees grow tall, which is why lumbering is mostly practised there.

The chapter's own classification supplies the industry that follows: forest-based industries process products from the forests, wood being made into paper or providing timber for various uses, along with resins, gums, colours, dyes, fragrant oils and turpentine.

Fishing and fish-processing would be expected on the coast as well, since the chapter's marine-based category covers the processing and canning of fish and fish products, and fig. 4.1 shows fishing grounds in those waters.

The Great Lakes gave the region cheap water transport and abundant water, which are two of the conditions the chapter names for industry.

The chapter lists large rivers and the Great Lakes among the physical factors affecting the localisation of industry in North America, and the development of inland water transport among the human factors.

Why that matters is set out in its account of transportation: the cost of transportation will be more for heavy, bulky raw materials and for longer distances, while such items can be brought from far distances through cheaper transportation like waterways. The lakes let iron ore and coal, both heavy and bulky, be carried between the mining areas and the mills at low cost.

Water supply reinforces it, since almost all industries require plenty of water for processes like cooling, smelting and washing, and the chapter notes that such industries are located near the banks of rivers or near lakes.

Once iron and steel works had gathered there, agglomeration did the rest: the chapter observes that all over the world, places where iron and steel industries were located saw the development of industries using steel as a raw material, such as utensils, automobile accessories and locomotives.

It made an otherwise unreachable region reachable.

The chapter lists a railway transport system among the human factors behind Russia's industrial regions, alongside government support and developed port facilities despite an inhospitable climate. It also names the Siberian Region and the Vladivostok Far East Industrial Region as industrial regions, and the map shows the Siberian Region as a long belt running west to east, which is the line the railway takes.

The reason a railway matters so much there follows from the chapter's own account of transportation: low cost of transportation is the key factor in the location of industries, and cost rises with weight and distance. Siberia's resources, which the chapter lists as nearness to coal fields, a large forest reserve, oil and gas, iron ore, gold, diamonds, tin and mercury, are all heavy or bulky and lie very far from any market, so without a railway none of them could be moved economically.

The railway also carried in the labour and supplies that a region with such a climate cannot provide for itself.

| A | B | C |
|---|---|---|
| 1) Small-scale industries | 1) Manual manufacturing | 1) Ceramics |
| 2) Cottage industries | 2) Skilled crafts person | 3) Potters |
| 3) Consumer goods | 4) Ready for direct consumption | 4) Pharmaceutical |
| 4) Private sector | 3) Individual ownership | 2) Tata Iron and Steel company |

Each chain runs from a class of industry, through what defines it, to an example.

Consumer goods and private sector come straight from the chapter. It defines consumer goods or light industries as those that manufacture goods ready for direct consumption, and names pharmaceutical plants among its examples. It defines private sector enterprise as one owned by a private individual or a partnership of private individuals, and gives the Tata Iron and Steel Company as the example.

The other two follow from the same logic. Cottage industries are the work of a skilled crafts person, and potters are the example. Small-scale industries are left with manual manufacturing and ceramics.

Because the factors that decide where an industry can be located are not the same everywhere.

The chapter states this directly: industries are unevenly distributed because the factors affecting industrial location are not the same everywhere, and industries tend to concentrate in a few pockets because of those favourable factors. The pockets with a high concentration are called industrial regions.

The factors it names are physical, economic, political and other. The physical ones are climate, availability of raw material, water and power supply, labour, transportation, and site or availability of land. The economic ones are proximity to market and capital. The political ones are government policies and the setting up of SEZs. Few places have all of them together.

Unevenness then feeds on itself. The chapter explains that capital is attracted to those areas where industries are localised, which in turn attracts more industries, and that by economies of scale a region with facilities attracts still more, until concentration or agglomeration occurs and the physical and economic factors no longer govern location at all.

Because iron and steel manufacture is tied to its raw material, and the raw material is there.

The chapter states that industries dependent on perishable, heavy, bulky and weight-losing raw materials are located near the raw material area. Iron ore and coal are both heavy and bulky, and a great weight of each is consumed for a smaller weight of steel, so carrying them any distance is costly.

Coal ties the industry down twice over. The chapter notes that coal is heavy and bulky, so industries dependent on coal as an energy resource are located near the mining area. Dhanbad lies in the coalfields of the Chhota Nagpur plateau, which the chapter's table names as one of India's industrial regions and credits with rich mineral resources.

Once established, such a centre grows by agglomeration. The chapter observes that all over the world, places where iron and steel industries were located saw the development of industries using steel as raw material.

[Note: the chapter names the Chhota Nagpur Plateau as an industrial region but does not mention Dhanbad itself, which appears only in this exercise question.]

Because the fruit will not travel.

The chapter states that industries dependent on perishable raw materials are located near the raw material area, and gives exactly this case: industries processing local fruits are found near Mahabaleshwar and Nagpur, because perishable fruits need to be processed soon and hence are located near those cities.

Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg are the Konkan's mango and cashew districts, so the raw material is produced there and must be processed before it spoils.

The cost of transport points the same way. The chapter notes that the cost of transportation will be more for heavy, bulky and perishable raw materials, so it is cheaper to move the processed product than the fruit.

Because southern South America has few of the conditions the chapter requires for industry, and those it has are concentrated in a small area.

The map bears the pattern out: in the whole continent only Venezuela, Eastern Brazil, S.E. Brazil, Argentina and Chile carry industrial regions, and the interior none at all.

Market is the first difficulty. Nearness to market is essential for quick disposal of manufactured goods, and the southern part of the continent is thinly peopled.

Capital is the second. The chapter notes that industries are located where banking and financial facilities are easily available, and that capital is attracted to areas where industries are already localised, which works against a region starting from little.

Transport is the third. Low cost of transportation is the key factor in the location of industries, and the mountains along the western side of the continent, together with the great distances of the interior, make it expensive.

The physical setting adds to it. The chapter observes that harsh climate is not much suitable for the establishment of industries, and southern South America runs from desert through high mountain to cold southern latitudes.

[Note: the chapter gives no account of South America's industrial geography, so the reasons above apply its general location factors to the distribution the map shows.]

A footloose industry is one whose location is not governed by the weight of its raw material or of its finished product.

The chapter explains that such industries produce goods that are lightweight and can easily be transported to the markets, and that most footloose industries produce low volume and high value outputs.

Because neither the raw material nor the product is bulky, neither of the usual rules applies: the industry is not pulled towards the raw material as a weight-losing industry is, nor towards the market as a weight-gaining one is. It can therefore be set up wherever other considerations suit, such as available land, labour or the owner's own convenience.

The chapter's example is a honey processing unit, whose location is not related to the weight of the raw material or the finished product, so it may equally well be set up in the village where the honeycombs are or in the city.

Public sector industries are owned by the State.

The chapter explains that the government makes all the investments and that the marketing of the goods produced is through government agencies. Its example is Bharat Heavy Electrical Limited (BHEL).

This is one of the chapter's five categories of ownership, alongside the private sector, owned by a private individual or partnership; the joint sector, owned and managed jointly by the government and individuals or by two or more governments; the cooperative sector, in which a group of individuals pool resources and share profits and losses; and multi-national corporations, whose operations extend to more than one country.

The chapter notes that a public-sector enterprise can also be an MNC, giving the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation, with headquarters in Dehradun, as an example.

Economies of scale, or agglomeration, is the process by which an industrial region grows because it is already industrial.

The chapter explains it in stages. The availability of various facilities leads to the establishment of industries in a region. By using the available opportunities according to economies of scale, the region attracts more industries with time. Consequently concentration or agglomeration of industries occurs there.

Its striking consequence is that the ordinary rules stop applying: the chapter states that as a result of this, the physical and economic factors have no influence on location.

A special characteristic of such a region is that industries mutually complementary to each other are established there. The chapter's example is that all over the world, places where iron and steel industries were located saw the development of industries which use steel as a raw material, such as utensils, automobile accessories and locomotives, which in turn led to car-manufacturing units, packaging industries and railway engine manufacturing industries.

Due to such agglomerations, new industries get more profit than they would elsewhere, which is what keeps drawing them in.

Transportation decides both where an industry can be and whether it can pay.

The chapter defines the key idea first: the cost of transportation and the time required to carry goods is known as economic distance, and low cost of transportation is the key factor in the location of industries.

Cost rises with weight and with distance. It will be more for heavy, bulky and perishable raw materials and for longer distances, transportation of coal being the example. That is what pins weight-losing industries near their raw material and perishable-fruit processing near the orchard.

Cheap transport releases an industry from that pull. Light-weight and non-perishable items can be brought from far distances through cheaper transportation like waterways, so such industries may be located near ports or rivers; the chapter gives cotton textiles and pulpwood as examples.

Transport is also a condition of the site itself. A location should be generally flat and well served by adequate transport facilities.

And it shapes whole regions. The chapter lists the development of inland water, rail transport and ports among the human factors behind North America's industrial regions, rail and road transport behind western Europe's, an efficient transportation system behind Japan's, an excellent rail network behind India's, and a railway transport system behind Russia's.

| Point of difference | Weight-losing industries | Weight-gaining industries |
|---|---|---|
| Raw material | Relatively bulky | Lighter |
| Finished product | Relatively lighter | Heavier and bulky |
| Where they are located | Near the raw material | Near the market |
| Why | Carrying the bulky raw material any distance is costly, so the processing is done where it is produced | Carrying the heavier product is costly, so it is made where it will be sold |
| Examples | Sugar mills and jute mills, which are concentrated close to the sources of raw material; fruit-processing near Mahabaleshwar and Nagpur | Bakery industries, since cake as a final product is heavier than the raw materials |

The chapter notes that in earlier times transportation costs increased with distance and with weight, which is the reason both rules exist. Between the two lies a third case: a footloose industry, whose location is related to the weight of neither.

| Point of difference | Primary activities | Secondary activities |
|---|---|---|
| What they do | The product is directly obtained from nature | Raw materials are processed and made into a more durable product |
| Relation to each other | They supply the raw material | The products of primary activities are used as their raw material |
| Value | The product is taken as nature yields it | They add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products |
| Examples | Hunting, gathering, animal husbandry, agriculture, fishing, lumbering, mining | Manufacturing, processing and construction (infrastructure) industries |
| Where the work is done | In the field, forest, mine or sea | In a factory, which the chapter defines as the place where conversion of products obtained from primary activities into final products takes place |
| What decides location | Physical conditions, chiefly climate and the presence of the resource | Raw material, market, transport, labour, capital, power and government policy together |

| Point of difference | Basic or heavy industries | Consumer goods or light industries |
|---|---|---|
| What they produce | Material which is in turn used by other industries | Goods that are ready for direct consumption |
| Who buys the output | Other industries | The consumer |
| Examples | The iron and steel industry, which makes steel for further use in the automobile, heavy machinery and other industries | Watch-making, electronic goods, textile mills and pharmaceutical plants |
| Scale and investment | Heavy, requiring large plant and capital | Lighter, and possible at smaller scale |

Both belong to the chapter's classification based on the nature of output, which also includes a third class between them: ancillary industries, which manufacture parts and components used by other industries for making heavy articles such as trucks, buses, railway engines and tractors, so that their final product is the raw material for another industry. Nails, tyres, iron sills and iron sheets are its examples.

The chapter lists six physical factors.

Climate. Harsh climate is not much suitable for the establishment of industries, and there may not be any industrial development in extremely hot, humid, dry or cold climate; the chapter instances the extreme climate of North-West or extreme North India. A moderate climate is congenial, as on the western coast. Climate can also be specific to an industry: cotton thread-making required a humid climate because thread breaks in dry climate, which is why the majority of cotton textile mills were concentrated in the coastal parts of Maharashtra and Gujarat. Artificial humidifiers are used in dry areas now, but they increase the cost of production. Changes in climate, such as chronic droughts, can affect industries too.

Availability of raw material. Raw materials come mainly from farms, mines, forests and fisheries, so location depends on their nature. Industries using perishable, heavy, bulky and weight-losing raw materials are located near the raw material area; jute mills and sugar mills are concentrated close to their sources, and fruit-processing industries are found near Mahabaleshwar and Nagpur.

Water and power supply. Almost all industries require plenty of water for cooling, smelting and washing, so they are located near rivers or lakes. Coal, oil and electricity are indispensable. Coal is heavy and bulky, so industries dependent on it are located near the mining area, whereas electricity and oil can be supplied through wires and pipelines over long distances, so industries dependent on them need not be.

Labour. Different industries need different labour: construction, mining and textiles need semi-skilled labour, while food-processing and ornament-making need skilled labour. Despite mechanisation some industries still need many workers, which is why labour colonies are found near large industries.

Transportation. The cost and time of carrying goods is economic distance, and low cost of transportation is the key factor in industrial location. Cost is higher for heavy, bulky and perishable materials and for longer distances, while light non-perishable items can come from far off by cheap waterways, so such industries may be near ports or rivers.

Site or availability of land. The site should generally be flat and well served by transport, and large areas are needed to build factories. Industries were once concentrated near urban areas, but because land there is scarce and dear there is now a tendency to set up in rural areas, as at Lote Parshuram in Chiplun and Chakan in Pune.

Sugar industries are located near the production of the raw material, and the reason lies in the cane itself.

The chapter states that sugarcane loses weight and amount of sugar after harvesting as the time after harvest increases, which affects its effective use for producing sugar, so sugarcane needs to be sent to nearby factories as soon as possible.

Sugarcane is therefore both perishable and weight-losing, and the chapter gives the rule for both: industries dependent on perishable, heavy, bulky and weight-losing raw materials are located near the raw material area, and weight-losing industries will be located near the raw material. It names sugar mills, with jute mills, among the industries mostly concentrated close to the sources of raw materials for this very reason.

Transport cost points the same way. The cost of transportation will be more for heavy, bulky and perishable raw materials and for longer distances, and cane is all three.

Beyond the cane, the ordinary factors apply. A sugar mill needs plenty of water for its processes, power to run it, semi-skilled labour, a flat site with room to build, and roads good enough for the cane to arrive quickly. The map of Solapur district in the chapter shows the result: a scatter of mills through the cane-growing area, each serving the fields around it.

Central Australia carries no industrial region on the map, and the chapter's location factors explain why between them.

Climate. The chapter states that harsh climate is not much suitable for the establishment of industries, and that there may not be any industrial development in extremely hot, humid, dry or cold climate. Central Australia is desert.

Water. Almost all industries require plenty of water for processes such as cooling, smelting and washing, and such industries are located near rivers or lakes. The interior has neither in any quantity.

Labour. Some industries still require a large number of workers despite mechanisation, and the interior is very thinly peopled.

Market. Nearness to market is essential for quick disposal of manufactured goods, and there is no market of any size in the interior. Every Australian industrial region the map names, Perth, Adelaide, Melbourne and Sydney, is coastal, where the population is.

Transport. Low cost of transportation is the key factor in the location of industries, and the interior is very far from any port, so both raw materials and finished goods would have to be carried great distances.

Agglomeration works against it as well. The chapter notes that capital is attracted to areas where industries are already localised, which in turn attracts more industries, so a region with none is at a standing disadvantage.

[Note: the chapter does not discuss Australia's interior specifically, so the reasons above apply its general location factors to the pattern fig. 5.3 shows.]

Mark the Ruhr region in western Germany, in western Europe. It is named on fig. 5.3 as the Ruhr Region.

Show it with an industrial symbol or shading and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

The chapter's table places it first among the industrial regions of western Europe, alongside parts of France, Great Britain and Italy, and gives its advantages as the River Rhine, large coal and iron reserves, natural harbours, skilled labour, a large market, port facilities and the development of rail and road transport. Its industries are named as ferrous and non-ferrous metal production and processing, petroleum, coal, cement, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and machine tools among others.

Mark any one of the three Japanese regions named on fig. 5.3: Tokyo-Kawasaki-Yokohama, Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto, or Nagoya and the northern Kyushu region. All three lie on the Pacific coast of the islands.

Show it with an industrial symbol or shading and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

The chapter's table names the same three, and gives their advantages as coastal plains, rich natural resource regions, availability of hydro power, a broken coastline and fast-flowing rivers, with an abundant supply of cheap labour, relatively developed infrastructure, market availability, an efficient transportation system and port facilities, noting that the port city of Yokohama facilitates trade.

Mark the Witwatersrand region in South Africa, which fig. 5.3 names, with Kimberley nearby.

Show it with an industrial symbol or shading and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

Both are mineral-based regions, which fits the chapter's rule that industries dependent on heavy and bulky raw materials are located near the raw material area, and its category of mineral-based industries, where manufacturing is based on mineral wealth obtained through mining.

[Note: the chapter's continent-wise table does not cover Africa, so the map is the source for this region.]

Mark any one of the Australian regions named on fig. 5.3: Perth, Adelaide, Melbourne or Sydney. All four lie on the coast.

Show it with an industrial symbol or shading and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

Their coastal position is itself the lesson of the map. The chapter's account of transportation notes that light non-perishable items can be brought from far distances through cheaper transportation like waterways, so such industries may be located near ports, and the interior of the continent, being desert and almost unpeopled, offers neither water, labour nor market.

[Note: the chapter's continent-wise table does not cover Australia, so the map is the source for these regions.]

Mark the region around the Great Lakes in the north-east of North America, between the United States and Canada. Fig. 5.3 names New England, New York, the Mid-Atlantic Region and southern Canada in and around it.

Show it with an industrial symbol or shading and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

The chapter's table lists large rivers and the Great Lakes among the physical factors behind North America's industrial regions, together with rich reserves of mineral resources, a broken coastline, and the location of North America and Europe facing each other across the Atlantic; and among the human factors, huge capital, a vast market, cheap and skilled labour, export facilities and the development of inland water, rail transport and ports.
